summary: Describes how IETF Integrated Services should be mapped onto LANs built from IEEE 802 segments joined by bridges or switches. It explains how service guarantees translate to the LAN's own traffic handling. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Fast-lane promises made by the big Internet need to work in your local network too. This explains how to carry those promises across the local network's own rules.

questions: how does intserv map to ethernet switches
what is the default user_priority mapping
subtitle: How IP service classes are mapped onto the eight 802.1 user_priority values that LAN switches understand.

tldr.problem: IETF Integrated Services describe flows with a multidimensional set of parameters, but switches that follow IEEE 802.1D only offer a handful of priority queues.
tldr.mechanism: Flows are grouped into traffic classes, each tagged with an 802.1D user_priority value. A default table maps delay targets to values, and the network chooses the class for each flow while an admission control element limits what each class carries.
tldr.outcome: Priority queuing plus admission control gives a close approximation of Controlled Load and, with much stricter admission control, Guaranteed Service. It cannot do per-flow policing, so policing is approximated at the network edge.

today: RFC 2815 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is one component of the Integrated Services over IEEE 802 LANs framework and is used with the signaling protocol in RFC 2814.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The IEEE 802.1 group extended the basic MAC service in bridged LANs (switched LANs). The updated IEEE 802.1D-1998 proposes differential traffic class queuing in switches, and IEEE 802.1Q lets Ethernet frames carry a traffic class indicator called user_priority inside the frame.

With that queuing plus admission control and signaling, IEEE 802 networks can closely approximate the IETF Integrated Services capabilities, namely Controlled Load and Guaranteed Service. This RFC maps the service classes and parameters of the IETF model onto IEEE 802.1D parameters. The signaling protocol that goes with it is the Subnet Bandwidth Manager in RFC 2814, and the overall framework is RFC 2816.
sections.eli5: Newer switches can sort the traffic into a few waiting lines, so some traffic goes first. This document explains which promise goes in which line.

sections.title: Aggregated Flows, Not Per-Flow Handling
sections.content:
One model would treat switches like routers, with the packet handling based on each RSVP flow, or by mapping each RSVP session onto something like an ATM virtual circuit. The RFC calls this inappropriate for IEEE 802. Filtering to the per-flow level gets expensive as switch speed rises, and such devices would be about as complex as IP routers.

Instead it uses an aggregated flow approach. Each arriving flow is assigned to one of the available classes for the duration of the flow. The border device (end host or border router) tags its traffic with a user_priority value, and flows with similar needs share a class. It works even with switches that have only the simplest 802.1D differential classification.

Who decides which class a flow uses? Defining universal class meanings in an RFC would be simple but too rigid. So clients ask the network, in a one-pass exchange piggybacked on the admission control request and answer, and the answer reflects topology, load and other admitted flows. All of a flow's packets keep the same class for its duration, which keeps them in order. The network must pick a class whose targets fit the flow and which has capacity left. The RFC chooses fixed class targets, because letting them change as flows come and go makes the packing problem hard.

The client can be an end station, an edge router, or a first switch acting as a proxy for a device that does not take part.
sections.eli5: Instead of giving every kid their own personal bus, the school sorts kids into a few buses by how much of a hurry they are in. Each kid stays on the same bus the whole trip.

sections.title: Choosing a Class and Bounding Delay
sections.content:
Admission control requests describe bandwidth, delay, jitter and service class, but the default 802 switch behavior is strict priority queuing, which is one-dimensional. Priority queuing alone gives only a relative ordering between classes. It cannot enforce a delay bound or tell flows apart inside a class. The RFC lists three things needed for absolute control of loss and delay:

  • Known bandwidth for QoS flows, with a limit on how many are admitted. A Subnet Bandwidth Manager provides this.
  • A scheduler giving preferential service to flows with lower delay targets. The user_priority mechanism provides this.
  • Protection of in-Tspec flows from best-effort traffic and from flows exceeding their Tspecs. A simple priority scheduler cannot police, so this is usually done at the network edge by a Layer 3 device, and it is therefore approximate.

It is the combination of priority scheduling and admission control that creates quantified delay bounds, and the admission algorithm decides which Integrated Services service is on offer. A relatively simple algorithm can give Controlled Load behavior. Guaranteed Service needs a much more stringent allocation and the computation of the C and D error terms. A delay bound has meaning only at the admission control element, which may cover a whole L2 domain or one segment, and end-to-end delay is found by summing along the path with the usual RSVP mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Lines alone only say who goes first. To promise 'you will wait no longer than this', someone must also count how many people are allowed in each line.

sections.title: Default user_priority Mappings
sections.content:
Table 1 gives the default mapping from delay targets to user_priority classes. The RFC stresses that these are defaults and must be changeable. The table is held by switches (and routers if desired) and generally not by end hosts, and it is read-write. The delay numbers are per-Bandwidth-Allocator targets drawn from a subjective look at voice and video needs, and nothing requires adherence to them.

Classes 4, 5 and 6 are suggested for delay-sensitive, admission-controlled flows, but any class above Best Effort could be used. A benefit is that a switch with two queues using the 802.1D default split of 0-3 and 4-7 gives all delay-sensitive traffic the high-priority queue. Network Control at class 7 protects route updates and management traffic, but it eats into assurances for other classes. So any device doing admission control, such as an SBM, must estimate the amount of Network Control traffic and use it in decisions for the lower classes.

Class 1, below Best Effort, could be used to penalty-tag all data of flows that exceed their allocation or Tspec. Tagging only the excess packets is often considered a bad idea, because it likely causes significant re-ordering of the flow.

The RFC does not dictate what mechanisms a switch uses to implement the mappings, and notes that devices with more complex scheduling than strict priority may be better served by more specialized mappings.
sections.eli5: There are eight lanes numbered 0 to 7. Lane 0 is the normal lane, higher lanes are faster, and the top lane is saved for the traffic cops' own messages.

sections.title: Characterization Parameters
sections.content:
Every Integrated Services network element must compute and expose characterization parameters, by calculation, measurement or estimation. In 802 networks it is nearly impossible to compute them exactly for some topologies, so simple switches may just describe themselves and admit flows conservatively.

The general parameters are the ingress link, egress links with their MTUs, framing overheads and minimum packet sizes, available path bandwidth, and minimum latency. MTU and minimum packet size must be reported accurately, and so must the break bits that show QoS support. Bandwidth can be a very loose estimate.

For Guaranteed Service an element must determine the constant delay bound (reported as the C parameter), the rate-proportional delay bound (D), and receive and transmit resources per flow. Estimates should err toward better performance than requested, so C and D should overestimate delay. Controlled Load exports no service-specific parameters, only internal resource estimates. A best-effort-only element needs no explicit parameters, though it sets the break bit.
sections.eli5: Each stop on a trip posts a small sign saying how big its doors are and how long it usually makes you wait. The signs may be rough, but they should lean toward saying it is slower than it really is.

sections.title: Merging Reservations
sections.content:
When reservations using the SBM TCLASS object are merged, the rule must be consistent with the user_priority mapping, and a merged reservation must get at least as good service as the best of its parts. No single rule avoids all side effects. Demoting an existing branch to a higher-delay class denies it service. Promoting it to a lower-delay class may fail admission or cost more. Promoting the new branch may make it fail for lack of resources in that class.

So such a merger is declared illegal and the usual SBM admission failure rules apply. The class is chosen from the TSpec when the first RESV for a flow arrives. If a second RESV reaches a branch point where the class would differ, an RSVP/SBM ResvErr goes back to the Layer 3 device that sent it, which passes it on under RSVP rules. If the classes are the same, the requests are merged and sent toward the senders. Detailed rules are in RFC 2814.
sections.eli5: If two friends want to join the same line, they must pick the same line. If they want different ones, the answer is no, instead of bumping people already waiting.

sections.title: Where the Mappings Apply
sections.content:
Layer 2 switches must interoperate with routers and Layer 3 switches in several arrangements: every device is Layer 3 capable, only edges are pure Layer 2, every other device lacks Layer 3, or most lack it apart from some control points. Equipment with no Integrated Services or 802.1D traffic management, which puts all packets through one queue, makes the service harder to support. Both service classes assume flows are policed and insulated from misbehaving flows, and with default user_priority devices this cannot be done inside the 802 network, so policing is approximated at the edge.

For Guaranteed Service all switching elements on the path must take part, and a path with even one switch transmitting onto a shared or half-duplex segment is unlikely to approximate it well. Controlled Load asks less, though differential queuing and buffering is still needed. The break bits tell users where such a gap exists. The RFC suggests sharing more neighbor capability information between switches, and notes the easiest solution of all is upgrading links and switches to higher capacities.
sections.eli5: A fast lane only works if every road along the way has one. If one road has no fast lane, the promise stops there.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Any use of QoS opens the possibility of denial of service or theft of service attacks, so it needs a security review. The RFC says it introduces no new security issues beyond those in its companion ISSLL documents, RFC 2816 and RFC 2814. It assumes that all requests for service are appropriately authenticated.
sections.eli5: Only people with a real ticket should be allowed into the fast lane.

items.desc: Default, assumed to be Best Effort.

items.label: Network Control
items.desc: Protects route updates and network management.

viz.caption: THREE THINGS NEEDED FOR ABSOLUTE LOSS AND DELAY CONTROL

items.title: Admission control
items.text: Know the bandwidth and limit how many flows are admitted. Done by a Subnet Bandwidth Manager.

items.title: Scheduling
items.text: Give preferential service to flows with lower delay targets using user_priority.

items.title: Policing
items.text: Keep best-effort and out-of-Tspec flows from hurting in-Tspec flows, approximated at the edge.
